flashcards.q: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
flashcards.a: Authentication checks who you are. Authorization decides whether you may do a particular action on a particular thing.
flashcards.more: At the courier office, showing your ID is authentication; matching the parcel to your name is authorization. Identity is checked once at the start of the request, but permission is checked separately for every thing. Passing one does not pass the other.

flashcards.q: What does IDOR mean?
flashcards.a: Getting someone else's data by changing an id in the URL or body, because the server never checked that the thing belongs to this user.
flashcards.more: The full name is Insecure Direct Object Reference; in the API world it is also called BOLA. If changing `/api/invoices/1042` to `1043` returns another user's invoice, that is IDOR. No tool is needed to exploit it, and every request looks normal in the server log, so it can go unnoticed for a long time.

flashcards.q: 401 versus 403: when do you use which?
flashcards.a: 401: no identity or invalid proof, so log in. 403: the identity is known, but this action is not allowed.
flashcards.more: On a 401, the client should send the user to the login page or refresh the token. On a 403, logging in again is pointless because the permission itself is missing. To hide that someone else's thing exists, many APIs return 404 instead of 403. That is acceptable as long as the same rule is used everywhere.

flashcards.q: Where do AuthN and AuthZ live in Symfony?
flashcards.a: AuthN: the firewall's authenticator. AuthZ: `access_control` (by URL), `#[IsGranted]` (by action) and voters (by object).
flashcards.more: An authenticator (such as `json_login`, `form_login` or `access_token`) finds the user from the request's cookie or token. Permission is then checked in three layers, from coarse to fine. The first two only understand roles; only a voter can check ownership of one specific object.

flashcards.q: What does a Symfony voter do?
flashcards.a: It answers a yes/no question: may this user do this action on this object? The rule lives in one place.
flashcards.more: A voter has two methods: `supports()` decides whether the question is its business, and `voteOnAttribute()` runs the actual rule. Writing `#[IsGranted('INVOICE_VIEW', subject: 'invoice')]` on a controller makes Symfony call the voter. More in [[security/authorization-models/role-explosion|authorization models]].

flashcards.q: How do you stop a list endpoint from leaking other people's data?
flashcards.a: Filter by the logged-in user (or their company) in the query itself, instead of fetching everything and filtering afterwards.
flashcards.more: Fetching every row and running a voter in a loop makes the query slow, breaks pagination counts, and leaks data the moment one condition is forgotten. A query like `findBy(['company' => $user->getCompany()])` never lets other people's rows out of the database at all.

flashcards.q: Is hiding a button in Vue a form of authorization?
flashcards.a: No, it only makes the UI nicer to use. The API can be called directly, so the real check must happen on the server, on every action.
flashcards.more: The user has full control over everything that runs in their browser: they can open DevTools and reveal a hidden button, or call the endpoint with curl. Hiding something in the UI only hides it from view. The server should treat every request as if a stranger wrote it.

flashcards.q: You put a voter on the GET action of an invoice. What else must you guard?
flashcards.a: Every other method too: PATCH, PUT and DELETE each need their own check. Attackers try every method on the same URL.
flashcards.more: It is very common to guard the read and forget the write. Give writes their own attributes (INVOICE_EDIT, INVOICE_DELETE) with rules at least as strict as viewing, and test them by trying the other methods as a different company.

flashcards.q: Does using a UUID as the id solve IDOR?
flashcards.a: No. A UUID makes guessing harder, but once an id leaks the data is open. You still need an ownership check.
flashcards.more: A UUID is not a secret. It travels in shared links, emails, logs, browser history and screenshots. Security should rest on "does this user have permission?", not on "does this user know the id?". A UUID is one extra hurdle, not a lock.

flashcards.q: What does deny by default mean?
flashcards.a: If no rule matches, the answer is "no". A new route is closed automatically, and opening it takes a deliberate decision.
flashcards.more: Symfony's `access_control` is open when no rule matches, so you end the list with a catch-all (`^/` → `IS_AUTHENTICATED_FULLY`). Then a new endpoint can't be left open by mistake. The opposite approach, everything open and closing routes one by one, creates a hole the moment you forget a route. The same goes for voters: when in doubt, return `false`.

flashcards.q: What is the core difference between a session and a JWT?
flashcards.a: A session keeps state on the server, and the client holds only an id. A JWT carries the data and a signature in the token itself, and the server remembers nothing.
flashcards.more: Think of the guest list at the door versus a printed ticket. Strike the name off the list and the slip is dead (session). Once a printed ticket has been handed out, you can't take it back (JWT).

flashcards.q: What is the biggest problem with JWTs?
flashcards.a: They are hard to revoke before they expire, because the server only checks the signature and remembers nothing.
flashcards.more: Even after a user is banned or logs out, an old JWT keeps working until it expires. That's why JWT lifetimes are kept short, and why a denylist or a token checked against the database is used when revocation is needed.

flashcards.q: Is a JWT payload secret?
flashcards.a: No. The payload is only base64-encoded, not encrypted, so anyone can read it. Never put confidential data in it.
flashcards.more: The signature only proves the data wasn't changed; it doesn't hide it. Paste any JWT into jwt.io and the payload is right there. Keep it to harmless data such as a user id and an expiry.

flashcards.q: What lifetimes do access and refresh tokens usually get?
flashcards.a: Access token: 5 to 15 minutes. Refresh token: a few days up to 30 days, stored hashed in the database and revocable.
flashcards.more: A short access token keeps the window of damage small if it's stolen. The long-lived refresh token lives in the database, so you can delete it directly on logout or ban.

flashcards.q: With a 15-minute access token, how long can a banned user still get in?
flashcards.a: Up to 15 minutes, until the access token expires. After that the deleted refresh token can't fetch a new one.
flashcards.more: That wait is the price of not asking the database on every request. If 15 minutes is too long, check the user or a denylist on each request, or use a server-side session. You then pay one read per request.

flashcards.q: What is refresh token rotation?
flashcards.a: Each refresh spends the old token and issues a new pair. If a spent token appears again, it was probably stolen.
flashcards.more: When reuse is detected, all of that user's tokens are revoked. The thief and the real user are both logged out, and the real user simply logs in again. This is the most common way to catch a stolen refresh token.

flashcards.q: Why is a refresh token stored hashed in the database?
flashcards.a: If the database leaks, the hash doesn't reveal the real token, just like a password.
flashcards.more: When the token is long and random enough (`random_bytes(32)`), a fast SHA-256 is enough and you don't need bcrypt. Passwords need a slow hash only because they have low entropy.

flashcards.q: Where should tokens be kept in the browser?
flashcards.a: The refresh token goes in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie. Not in localStorage, because an XSS script can read it.
flashcards.more: If you like, keep the access token in JavaScript memory (Pinia state); after a page reload, get a new one with the refresh token in the cookie. That leaves nothing on disk for a script to read.

flashcards.q: What does the SameSite=Strict cookie attribute prevent?
flashcards.a: The cookie is not sent on requests that start from another site, which makes CSRF attacks harder.
flashcards.more: With Strict, even the first request arriving from an outside link carries no cookie; Lax sends it on safe GET navigations. For state-changing requests, use at least Lax.

flashcards.q: What is OAuth2 for, and what is it not for?
flashcards.a: OAuth2 is for granting permission (authorization): what an app may do. Telling you who the user is is not its job.
flashcards.more: OAuth2 issues an access token, which tells an API "this request is valid for such-and-such scope". Using it alone as proof of login is a mistake, because the app can't tell who it was issued for. For identity, use OIDC.

flashcards.q: What does OIDC add on top of OAuth2?
flashcards.a: An id_token (a JWT) stating who the user is (sub, email), plus the `openid` scope and rules for a verified login.
flashcards.more: OIDC = OAuth2 + identity. It isn't a separate protocol: add `openid` to the scope of the same flow and you also get an id_token. Google, Microsoft and Okta all support it.

flashcards.q: What are the four roles in OAuth2?
flashcards.a: Resource owner (the user), client (the app), authorization server (issues tokens), resource server (the API that accepts tokens).
flashcards.more: In the building-guard metaphor: Ryan is the owner, the courier is the client, the guard is the authorization server, and the mailbox is the resource server. In a small system the authorization and resource servers may belong to the same company, but the roles stay distinct.

flashcards.q: What is SAML, and when do you need it?
flashcards.a: SAML is an older XML-based SSO protocol. You need it when an enterprise customer wants employees to log in through their own IdP (Okta, AD FS).
flashcards.more: OIDC and SAML solve the same problem: a central IdP verifies identity and tells the app. SAML sends a signed XML assertion, OIDC sends a JWT. OIDC is simpler for new projects, but if you sell B2B software, expect customers to ask for SAML.

flashcards.q: What does PKCE prevent?
flashcards.a: Getting tokens with a stolen authorization code. Only the app that started the flow holds the original code_verifier.
flashcards.more: At the start the app creates a random `code_verifier` and sends its SHA-256 hash (`code_challenge`). At the end, when it shows the verifier, the server hashes it and compares. It is mandatory for public clients and now recommended for all clients.

flashcards.q: Why does OAuth need a state parameter?
flashcards.a: To prevent CSRF. If the returned state doesn't match the one stored in the session, we never started that request.
flashcards.more: Without state, an attacker can push the code from their own account into a victim's browser. The state is random every time, bound to the session, and deleted after one use.

flashcards.q: Which four id_token claims must always be verified?
flashcards.a: `iss` (who issued it), `aud` (is it our client_id), `exp` (expiry), `nonce` (is it for this login attempt).
flashcards.more: Skip any one and a token meant for another app, or an old one, can log someone in. If the token arrives through the browser, you must also verify its signature against the JWKS. Use `sub`, not the email, as the user's stable key.

flashcards.q: Why must redirect_uri be registered exactly?
flashcards.a: With a wildcard, an open redirect can send the code or token to an attacker's URL.
flashcards.more: The IdP only sends the code to a URL registered in advance. If you register `https://app.com/*`, an attacker who finds any redirect hole in the app can steer the code to themselves. Register the full URL, separately for each environment.

flashcards.q: What is RBAC, and where does it run out?
flashcards.a: Role-based access control: permission by the user's title. It is simple, but once department, amount or ownership conditions arrive, roles explode in number.
flashcards.more: For a small app, `ROLE_USER` and `ROLE_ADMIN` are enough. But making a separate role for each condition such as "own department" or "under $500" makes the count multiply. That is when it is time to move to ABAC.

flashcards.q: What does ABAC mean?
flashcards.a: Attribute-based access control: the decision combines facts about the user, the thing and the environment (department, amount, time).
flashcards.more: In Symfony, ABAC means a voter with conditions like `$subject->getDepartment() === $user->getDepartment()`. The role is only the coarse door; the fine rules come from the data.

flashcards.q: What does ReBAC mean?
flashcards.a: Relationship-based: permission comes from the user's relationship to the thing (editor, owner, member), with inheritance.
flashcards.more: In Google Drive, being an editor of a folder makes you an editor of the files inside. Google's Zanzibar is built on this idea, and OpenFGA is its open-source counterpart. In a small app you can do it easily with a Symfony voter and a grants table.

flashcards.q: What is a policy engine, and when do you need one?
flashcards.a: A tool that decides from rules written outside your code, in a separate language (Rego, Cedar). Use it for the same rules across many services, or to change rules without deploying.
flashcards.more: OPA, Cedar and OpenFGA are examples. But for one Symfony monolith with a few rules, voters are enough; another service is another place to fail. Don't add an engine before you need one.

flashcards.q: What does a role hierarchy do in Symfony?
flashcards.a: It puts one role above another so the higher role gets all the lower one's permissions: `ROLE_MANAGER: ROLE_EMPLOYEE`.
flashcards.more: It is written under `role_hierarchy` in `security.yaml`, so you don't have to give a manager the employee role separately. But a role hierarchy only gives coarse permission; decisions about a specific thing belong in a voter.

flashcards.q: What do `supports()` and `voteOnAttribute()` do in a voter?
flashcards.a: `supports()` decides whether the question is this voter's business. `voteOnAttribute()` runs the real rule and returns true or false.
flashcards.more: An app has many voters; Symfony asks each one `supports()` and counts the votes only of those that say yes. `#[IsGranted('EXPENSE_APPROVE', subject: 'expense')]` calls this machinery directly.

flashcards.q: What does deny by default mean in a voter?
flashcards.a: For an unrecognized attribute or when in doubt, a voter always returns false. A permission must be earned by matching a rule on purpose.
flashcards.more: End your `match` or `if` chain with `default => false`. If the default is "yes", adding a new attribute later gives everyone permission by mistake.

flashcards.q: What goes wrong if roles are packed into the token at login?
flashcards.a: After a demotion or dismissal the old token still lists the old role, so the person keeps those powers until the token expires.
flashcards.more: Sarah is demoted at 10:00, but her 09:30 token still says manager for another hour. Read the user's current roles from the database on each request, or keep tokens short. The price is one user read per request.

flashcards.q: What is separation of duties?
flashcards.a: The person who requests an action can't approve it themselves. For example, an employee can't pass their own expense.
flashcards.more: It reduces both mistakes and fraud. In a voter, `$subject->getRequester() !== $user` is a simple condition. Keep this rule at every money-related or approval step.

flashcards.q: What is multi-tenancy?
flashcards.a: One piece of software serving many customers (tenants), with each customer's data kept separate from the others.
flashcards.more: This is the core design of SaaS: one codebase, one deploy, many companies. The hard parts are keeping everyone's data apart and making sure nobody uses up everyone else's resources.

flashcards.q: What are the three levels of tenant isolation?
flashcards.a: Row-level (a tenant_id in shared tables), schema-per-tenant, and database-per-tenant. The more separation, the more security and cost.
flashcards.more: The comparison: a bunk in a hostel room, an apartment in a building, a separate house. Most SaaS products start row-level and give a separate database to large or strictly regulated customers.

flashcards.q: What is the biggest risk of row-level tenancy?
flashcards.a: Forgetting the `tenant_id` condition in a single query leaks every tenant's data. You can't rely on remembering it by hand.
flashcards.more: That is why the condition is automated, with a Doctrine filter or database row-level security. Wherever security rests on one person's memory, a gap will eventually appear.

flashcards.q: What does a Doctrine SQL filter do?
flashcards.a: It adds an SQL condition (such as `tenant_id = 7`) to every DQL query automatically, so developers don't have to write it.
flashcards.more: `SQLFilter::addFilterConstraint()` is called for each entity and returns a piece of SQL. At the start of the request you enable it with `$em->getFilters()->enable('tenant')` and set the tenant using `setParameter`.

flashcards.q: Where should the tenant id come from?
flashcards.a: From the verified data of the logged-in user, never from the request's query, body or headers.
flashcards.more: What the client sends is a claim, not proof. Change `?tenant=7` to `8` and someone else's data would appear. The server itself knows which tenant the user belongs to.

flashcards.q: Why must new rows get their tenant stamped, and where?
flashcards.a: The filter only trims reads. A prePersist listener copies the logged-in user's tenant onto each new row; a row with no tenant would vanish.
flashcards.more: `tenant_id = 7` never matches NULL, so an unstamped row is invisible to every company. Take the tenant from the verified user, never from the request, and add NOT NULL in the database as a last guard.

flashcards.q: What is a noisy neighbor?
flashcards.a: One tenant using so many resources (CPU, database, requests) that the other tenants slow down.
flashcards.more: The risk is highest in row-level tenancy, where everyone shares one database. To contain it, use a per-tenant rate limit, separate queues or worker shares, and timeouts on heavy queries.

flashcards.q: What is the benefit of keying the rate limit by tenant?
flashcards.a: Each tenant is counted separately, so one customer's excess requests don't reduce another customer's share.
flashcards.more: In Symfony's RateLimiter, `$factory->create($tenantId)` gives each tenant its own bucket. This also makes it possible to give customers on bigger plans a higher limit.

flashcards.q: Where does the Doctrine filter not work?
flashcards.a: Raw DBAL SQL, native queries, and often background workers or console commands, where there is no request.
flashcards.more: In those places you carry the tenant by hand: put the tenantId in the message, enable the filter in the handler, write `tenant_id = :t` in raw SQL, and include the tenant in cache keys and unique indexes too.

flashcards.q: Why is account recovery a prime target for attackers?
flashcards.a: Because it is a way into the account without the password. However strong login is, a weak recovery path is the back door.
flashcards.more: Reset, changing the email, switching off MFA, asking support: all of these are recovery. Attackers look for the weakest path, so keep these as hard as the front door.

flashcards.q: What are the four properties of a good reset token?
flashcards.a: Random (from a CSPRNG), stored hashed in the database, short-lived (such as 30 minutes), and single-use.
flashcards.more: Generate it with `bin2hex(random_bytes(32))`, store `hash('sha256', ...)` in the database, set an expiry, and mark it used when it is spent. Miss any one and the attack comes through that gap.

flashcards.q: What should you not use to generate a reset token?
flashcards.a: `md5(email)`, `uniqid()`, `rand()`, the time or a user id. They are all guessable. Use `random_bytes()`.
flashcards.more: `random_bytes()` uses the operating system's secure random source (a CSPRNG). `rand()` and `uniqid()` depend on the time and can be guessed.

flashcards.q: What is user enumeration, and how do you prevent it?
flashcards.a: Learning who your users are by checking whether an email exists. Prevent it by always giving the same message, in the same time.
flashcards.more: The gap shows up in three places: forgot-password, login and signup. If you hand the real work to Messenger and return the same message in the response, even the response time reveals nothing.

flashcards.q: Where should the host of a reset link come from?
flashcards.a: From configuration (`framework.router.default_uri`), not from the request's Host header.
flashcards.more: If an attacker sends a changed Host header, the emailed link can carry his site's name, and the victim who clicks it hands over the token. This is called Host header poisoning. A host taken from config closes that gap.

flashcards.q: What else must be revoked when a password is reset?
flashcards.a: All the user's other sessions, refresh tokens and remember-me cookies. Then send a "your password was changed" email.
flashcards.more: In Symfony, changing the password hash invalidates other sessions on its own. Refresh tokens are separate, so you must revoke them yourself. Otherwise a thief who was already logged in stays in after the change.

flashcards.q: How do you make a reset token truly single-use when two requests arrive at once?
flashcards.a: Claim it with one atomic UPDATE ... WHERE used_at IS NULL AND expires_at > now, and proceed only if exactly one row changed.
flashcards.more: "Read the row, check it is unused, then mark it used" has a gap between the check and the write, and two simultaneous requests can both pass. A single conditional UPDATE lets the database pick one winner; the other changes zero rows.

flashcards.q: How should a reset handle MFA?
flashcards.a: MFA stays on after a reset. If MFA is lost, it is restored through recovery codes, or through a waiting period and warning messages.
flashcards.more: Switching MFA off with just an email link means that once the email is taken, everything is lost. Hand out 10 one-time recovery codes (stored hashed) in advance. If there are none, impose a 24 to 72 hour wait and email every address.

flashcards.q: Why does a recovery endpoint need a rate limit?
flashcards.a: Otherwise an attacker can send links to a thousand emails or brute-force a short (6-digit) code. Limit by both IP and email.
flashcards.more: In Symfony's RateLimiter you can build one limiter by IP and another by email. Past the limit you return 429 with `Retry-After`. This stops email bombing and guessing alike.

flashcards.q: What is a secret? Give three examples.
flashcards.a: Information that lets whoever knows it act as you: a password, an API key, a token, a private key.
flashcards.more: What separates a secret from ordinary configuration is the damage a leak causes. If `APP_ENV=prod` leaks, nothing happens, but if the password in `DATABASE_URL` leaks, someone else owns your database. That's why the two are handled differently.

flashcards.q: Why is committing a secret to a private repository still wrong?
flashcards.a: Every member of the repository, the CI system and every clone can see it, and it stays in history forever.
flashcards.more: Private only means outsiders can't see it. Every insider's laptop has the full history. A single incident (someone makes the repository public, a laptop is stolen) leaks everything. Keeping secrets apart from code is the right habit.

flashcards.q: You accidentally pushed a secret to git. What do you do first?
flashcards.a: Revoke it and create a new one (rotate). Deleting the commit is not enough, because it may already have been copied.
flashcards.more: The order is: 1) bring the new secret online, 2) revoke the old one, 3) check the logs to see whether anyone used it. Afterwards you can scrub it from history for tidiness, but that is for discipline, not for security.

flashcards.q: How does the Symfony secrets vault work?
flashcards.a: Secrets are encrypted with a public key and stored in git. Only the production private key can decrypt them.
flashcards.more: `secrets:set` encrypts the value and writes files under `config/secrets/<env>/`, which are safe to commit. In production the app decrypts them using the `prod.decrypt.private.php` file or `SYMFONY_DECRYPTION_SECRET`. If the private key reaches git, the vault is worthless.

flashcards.q: Which vault key must never go into git?
flashcards.a: The production decrypt private key (prod.decrypt.private.php).
flashcards.more: The public key (`prod.encrypt.public.php`) and the encrypted files can be committed. But whoever gets the decrypt private key can read every secret. So it stays in `.gitignore` and reaches the production server by a separate route.

flashcards.q: What is the Symfony way to read a secret from env inside a service?
flashcards.a: Put `#[Autowire(env: 'STRIPE_SECRET_KEY')]` on the constructor parameter.
flashcards.more: That way the secret's value never appears in the code, and one line shows where the service gets it from. `.env` holds only defaults or empty values; the real value comes from the vault or the production environment.

flashcards.q: What is secret rotation, and how do you do it without downtime?
flashcards.a: Create a new secret, roll it out everywhere, then revoke the old one. New first, old last.
flashcards.more: A deploy doesn't switch every server at the same instant, so for a while both keys must stay valid. For a DB password, create a new user, move the app to it, then disable the old user. Rotating regularly also shortens how long a leak can hurt you.

flashcards.q: What does least privilege mean?
flashcards.a: Give each key or user exactly as much power as its job needs, and no more.
flashcards.more: If the app's DB user is root, a SQL injection can wipe the whole database. If it only has SELECT/INSERT/UPDATE on the tables it needs, the same bug does far less damage. And when every service has its own key, one leak leaves the rest safe.

flashcards.q: An attacker is using your leaked key right now. Do you still rotate "new first, old last"?
flashcards.a: No. Revoke the key at once and accept a short outage. "New first" is for leaks nobody has used yet.
flashcards.more: Every minute the old key stays valid, the attacker keeps spending your money or reading your data. A few minutes of downtime costs less than that. Once the key is dead, bring the new one up, then look through the logs for what was done with it.

flashcards.q: A customer changes the order id in the URL and sees someone else's order. What is the fix?
flashcards.a: An object-level check: a voter confirms the order belongs to the logged-in user, so someone else's id gets a 403.
flashcards.more: Being logged in only proves who the customer is, not that this order is theirs. Asking "what if they send another id?" on design day turns the check into part of the feature, one `#[IsGranted]` line, instead of an emergency patch after a leak.

flashcards.q: What is threat modeling?
flashcards.a: Thinking before you build a feature: what could go wrong, who could cause harm, and what you will do about it.
flashcards.more: It is a design discussion, not a code review. You sketch a few boxes and arrows on paper and ask "what happens if someone does the opposite here?" That catches holes before launch, when fixing them is cheapest.

flashcards.q: When is the best time to do a threat model?
flashcards.a: At design time, before the code is written. Changing a design after launch costs far more.
flashcards.more: Data structures, APIs and trust boundaries are settled on design day. Changing them later touches many places. So a half-hour discussion at design time pays off the most.

flashcards.q: What is a trust boundary?
flashcards.a: The line between two zones, where data moves between places of different trustworthiness.
flashcards.more: Browser to API, API to an outside payment gateway, gateway back to our webhook: all of these cross a line. Like the doors in a bank, each one needs a check. Even data coming from an inner zone shouldn't be trusted blindly.

flashcards.q: What do the six letters of STRIDE stand for?
flashcards.a: Spoofing, Tampering, Repudiation, Information disclosure, Denial of service, Elevation of privilege.
flashcards.more: In plain words: faking identity, altering data, denying an action, leaking information, taking the service down, and gaining power you shouldn't have. Asking all six at every arrow catches most serious threats.

flashcards.q: How do Spoofing and Elevation of privilege differ?
flashcards.a: Spoofing is pretending to be someone else. Elevation is gaining power under your own identity that you shouldn't have.
flashcards.more: Authentication (who are you) stops spoofing. Authorization (what may you do) stops elevation. Logging in with a stolen password is spoofing. A normal user changing the URL to reach an admin page is elevation.

flashcards.q: What do you do to prevent Repudiation?
flashcards.a: Keep an audit log of who did what, when and to which thing, stored so it can't be altered.
flashcards.more: For important actions like refunds or settings changes, record the actor id, the time and the old and new values. It helps if the log is append-only, so entries can't be edited or deleted. Then nobody can get away with "I didn't do it".

flashcards.q: What are the four steps of a threat model?
flashcards.a: Draw (boxes, arrows, boundaries), hunt (STRIDE), decide (countermeasure or acceptance), verify (tests and tickets).
flashcards.more: The whole thing takes half an hour at a whiteboard. The output is a list of threats and a decision for each. Keep it in a document and it is useful again whenever the feature changes.

flashcards.q: Must you block every threat?
flashcards.a: No. Each one needs a decision: block it, reduce it, or accept it and write down why.
flashcards.more: When the damage is small and the likelihood is low, the countermeasure may cost more than the risk. Then you can accept it, but you must write down why. If you don't, someone later will think nobody noticed it.

flashcards.q: Why do you need server-side validation even if the browser already validates?
flashcards.a: Because an attacker can skip the browser and send requests directly. The client's check is for convenience, the server's is for security.
flashcards.more: Anyone can send any value straight to the API with curl or Postman. A Vue form shows mistakes quickly, but it can't stop anyone. With a DTO and constraints on the server, every request is checked by the same rules.

flashcards.q: What can happen if an order endpoint doesn't validate quantity?
flashcards.a: Someone sends quantity -5 with curl, the total goes negative, and the store owes money. A Range(min: 1, max: 10) constraint refuses it with a 422.
flashcards.more: The value must pass both the type (an int, not the string "abc") and the limits. A DTO with constraints checks both before your order code runs, so the rest of the code can trust what it receives.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between an allowlist and a blocklist, and which is better?
flashcards.a: An allowlist says what passes and rejects the rest. A blocklist says what is refused and lets the rest through. The allowlist is safer.
flashcards.more: With a blocklist, an attacker finds some form you never thought of. With an allowlist, everything unfamiliar is dropped automatically. In Symfony, `Assert\Choice`, `Assert\Range` and a host allowlist are all examples of this idea.

flashcards.q: What is the correct way to prevent SQL injection?
flashcards.a: Parameterized queries: the SQL is one thing, the value is a separate parameter. Never glue input into a string.
flashcards.more: `setParameter('email', $email)` or DBAL's `['email' => $email]` sends the value to the database on a separate path, so it never becomes an instruction. Escaping or a blocklist can't be trusted. Even with an ORM, gluing in a raw string is the same trap.

flashcards.q: What do you do when a user supplies the column name for ORDER BY?
flashcards.a: It can't be a parameter, so match it against an allowlist of approved columns and insert only that.
flashcards.more: A parameter can fill in only a value, not a column or table name. So compare `$sort` with `['price', 'created_at']`, and use a default if it doesn't match. Never put a user's string directly into SQL.

flashcards.q: What is XSS (cross-site scripting)?
flashcards.a: A script written by an attacker running in another user's browser as if it were part of the site.
flashcards.more: If you don't escape a comment or a name when placing it on the page, the browser treats it as HTML and runs it. That script can then steal a session or token and act as the user. Twig's and Vue's `{{ }}` escape by default.

flashcards.q: Which two features are the main doors to XSS?
flashcards.a: Vue's `v-html` and Twig's `|raw`: both turn escaping off and run user-written text as HTML.
flashcards.more: If you truly must display rich text, sanitize it on the server with HtmlSanitizer, keep only safe tags, and then show it. Add a CSP header on top, which blocks inline scripts, so even one mistake does limited damage.

flashcards.q: Should rich-text comments be cleaned in the browser or on the server?
flashcards.a: On the server, at save time, with HtmlSanitizer. A browser-only cleaner such as DOMPurify protects just that one client.
flashcards.more: A mobile app or an email that shows the same comment would still get the raw HTML. Cleaning once on the server covers every client; keep DOMPurify as a second layer if you like. The price is a few lines of config and one sanitize() call.

flashcards.q: What is SSRF, and in which features does it show up most?
flashcards.a: The server sends a request to a user-supplied URL and ends up reaching the internal network. Image import, webhook URLs, link previews.
flashcards.more: The most dangerous target is the cloud metadata address (169.254.169.254), which hands out the server's access keys. The remedies: a host allowlist, blocking private IPs (`NoPrivateNetworkHttpClient`), turning off redirects, and an egress firewall.

flashcards.q: Why is unsafe deserialization dangerous?
flashcards.a: unserialize() builds objects of any class the attacker picks, and their magic methods can run code as soon as it happens.
flashcards.more: PHP methods like `__destruct` and `__wakeup` run on their own when an object is created or destroyed. An attacker finds a chain of such methods inside the app's or a library's classes and runs malicious code. The fix: take untrusted data as JSON and map it onto a DTO.

flashcards.q: Why can't the client-supplied name and type be trusted in a file upload?
flashcards.a: The client can change both. Verify the real type from the content, and generate the name yourself.
flashcards.more: Sending shell.php labeled as image/jpeg is easy. So Symfony's `Assert\Image` or `Assert\File` judge the type from the content. Give the file your own UUID name, set a size limit, and store it outside the web root.

flashcards.q: What is the idea of keeping the damage limited even if the database is stolen?
flashcards.a: Defense in depth: protect the data itself (hash, encryption, tokens), so even if the outer wall falls the thief can't read anything.
flashcards.more: A firewall and passwords only block the way in. But backups, SQL injection and an employee's mistake can send data outside. So the data's own protection works as the last wall.

flashcards.q: What is the key difference between hashing and encryption for passwords?
flashcards.a: Encryption can be reversed with a key; a hash can't. A password only has to be matched, never read back.
flashcards.more: At login, the password the user typed is hashed again and compared with the stored hash. So the original password never has to be kept anywhere. If you encrypt instead, one stolen key opens every password at once.

flashcards.q: Why are MD5 or SHA-256 wrong for passwords?
flashcards.a: They are fast. An attacker can make billions of guesses per second and crack the passwords. A password hash must be deliberately slow.
flashcards.more: argon2id and bcrypt deliberately spend time and memory, so each guess is expensive. They also include a salt, so the same password gives a different hash each time and precomputed lists (rainbow tables) don't work.

flashcards.q: What is the right way to hash passwords in Symfony?
flashcards.a: Set `auto` under `password_hashers` and use `UserPasswordHasherInterface::hashPassword()`.
flashcards.more: `auto` picks the best algorithm available on the server. If the best algorithm changes later, old hashes upgrade themselves at login. The salt doesn't need separate storage; it lives inside the hash string.

flashcards.q: What do TLS, disk encryption and field encryption each stop?
flashcards.a: TLS: eavesdropping on the way. Disk: theft of a disk or backup. Field: a database leak and SQL injection.
flashcards.more: Each layer is for a different danger, and none replaces another. A running database reads the disk in the clear, so disk encryption does nothing against SQL injection. The most sensitive fields need app-level encryption.

flashcards.q: Why does sodium secretbox need a new nonce every time?
flashcards.a: Using the same nonce twice with the same key breaks the encryption. So use a random nonce each time and store it with the ciphertext.
flashcards.more: A nonce isn't secret; it just must be used once. It is attached to the front of the ciphertext so it is available when decrypting. secretbox is authenticated, so if anyone alters the data, decryption fails.

flashcards.q: What is envelope encryption?
flashcards.a: Data is encrypted with a data key, and that data key is locked by the master key in a KMS.
flashcards.more: The master key never leaves the KMS. The app asks the KMS to create or unlock data keys. To rotate the master key you only lock the data keys again; you don't re-encrypt all the data.

flashcards.q: How is envelope-encrypted data read back?
flashcards.a: The app sends the locked data key to the KMS, gets the open data key back, decrypts the data with it, then wipes the key from memory.
flashcards.more: Only the small data key travels to and from the KMS, never the data. Each decrypt is a network call to the KMS, so cache the data key briefly if you read often. That call is the price of keeping the master key out of your app.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between tokenization and masking?
flashcards.a: With tokenization the real value stays with the provider and we keep a token. Masking only hides part of a value when it is shown.
flashcards.more: Masking (***-**-6789) is for display or logs, not for protecting data. With tokenization our database never holds the real card number at all, so a leak costs us nothing and our PCI burden shrinks.

flashcards.q: How does personal data get into logs, and what stops it?
flashcards.a: A debug line that logs the whole request copies passwords and SSNs into log files. Log only the event (IP, reason, request id).
flashcards.more: Add a redacting processor as a safety net, and give logs a retention period and limited access. Logs are copied to search tools and backups, so a leaked log is a leaked database.

flashcards.q: What can a log redactor that matches key names not catch?
flashcards.a: Personal data inside the message text, or under a key name that isn't on its list. Keep PII out of messages and extend the list.
flashcards.more: A redactor like the one in this lesson only walks the context array and compares key names. `$logger->info("Login for $phone failed")` passes straight through, as does a key called `passport`. It is a safety net behind careful logging, not a replacement for it.

flashcards.q: What is a supply chain attack?
flashcards.a: An attempt to get into your system by slipping malicious code into an outside library or tool that you use.
flashcards.more: Instead of attacking your app directly, the attacker takes over someone in your dependencies' accounts or publishes a fake package. The malicious code then arrives in your app on its own with a new version. So adding a library means adding one more thing you trust.

flashcards.q: What is a transitive dependency?
flashcards.a: A library that a library you installed depends on. You didn't ask for it directly, yet it runs.
flashcards.more: When you `composer require` one package, its dependencies land in vendor/ too. `composer why <package>` tells you who pulled it in. To judge your risk, looking only at the list you installed yourself is not enough.

flashcards.q: Why do you commit composer.lock?
flashcards.a: So every build, test and production uses exactly the same versions of each library.
flashcards.more: Without a lock file, `composer install` looks for the newest versions, and what you tested and what gets deployed can differ. By checking the versions in the lock file, you can find out which versions have vulnerabilities.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between `composer install` and `composer update` in CI?
flashcards.a: `install` fetches the versions in the lock file. `update` pulls the newest versions and changes the lock file.
flashcards.more: `update` should run on a developer's machine, in a separate PR where people can review the change. In CI and production deploys, always use `install`.

flashcards.q: What does `composer audit` do?
flashcards.a: It checks the packages in the lock file against a list of known vulnerabilities (security advisories). If it finds any, the exit code is non-zero.
flashcards.more: Running `composer audit --locked` in CI breaks the build when a vulnerable package is present, so you learn about it at once. For the frontend, Yarn's audit has to be run separately. And an audit only catches known vulnerabilities, not new discoveries.

flashcards.q: What are three rules for keeping CI pipeline secrets safe?
flashcards.a: Short-lived (OIDC) credentials, least privilege, and giving secrets only to protected branches.
flashcards.more: A long-lived access key kept in CI keeps working for years if it is stolen. With OIDC, each run gets a credential good for about an hour. Never hand secrets to code you haven't reviewed, and never echo a secret.

flashcards.q: Does a PR from a fork get your secrets under the `pull_request` trigger?
flashcards.a: No: GitHub withholds secrets and makes the token read-only. The danger is `pull_request_target` that checks out the PR's code.
flashcards.more: `pull_request_target` runs the base repo's workflow with its secrets, even for a fork PR. If the job then checks out and runs the PR's code (composer scripts, tests), a stranger's code holds your keys. Keep untrusted code in a no-secrets workflow, and deploy in a separate one.

flashcards.q: Why do you pin a GitHub Actions action by commit SHA?
flashcards.a: The owner can move a tag (like v4), but can't change a SHA. A SHA always runs the same code.
flashcards.more: A third-party action runs in your CI with your secrets. If the owner's account is taken over, they can move the tag and put malicious code behind it. If you pin the SHA, you change it deliberately, and with your eyes open, when you update.

flashcards.q: Which two GDPR rules put the most pressure on design?
flashcards.a: Users' right to have their data erased and exported, and reporting a breach to the authority within 72 hours.
flashcards.more: The first means you must know everywhere the data lives and build an anonymize or delete feature. The second means writing a breach runbook in advance. It is a condition of the law.

flashcards.q: What is the easiest way to shrink the scope of PCI DSS?
flashcards.a: Don't bring card data onto your own server: use the payment provider's hosted form and tokens.
flashcards.more: Any system that touches card data falls under the PCI rules. So if you use the provider's form and take only a token on the server, your responsibility shrinks a lot. A CVV can never be stored after authorization.
